To share a complex report query that needs no input parameters, choose a {{c1::view}}.
column2:
Define the common query once and reference the view in FROM. If callers need to pass inputs to the object itself, consider a table-valued function.
Review source

column1: For read-only access through an updatable view, grant {{c1::SELECT}} without effective data-modification permissions.
column2:
SELECT allows reads without granting INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. Check effective permissions because membership in another role can still grant a write path.
Review source

column1: When adapting a view after a compatible change to its source, keep a {{c1::stable output interface}} so reports keep working.
column2:
Reports can keep querying the same column names and types while the view adapts to a compatible change in its source tables.
Review source

column1: A view modification that changes several base tables can be implemented with an {{c1::INSTEAD OF trigger}}.
column2:
The trigger receives the requested row changes and decides how to write them to the base tables. The ordinary view write does not run first.
Review source

column1: For an explicitly called order workflow that updates multiple tables in one transaction, choose a {{c1::stored procedure}}.
column2:
The procedure groups the workflow behind one call. Use an explicit transaction and error handling to make the changes succeed or fail together.
Review source

column1: Use a stored procedure when the caller needs named {{c1::OUTPUT parameters}} in addition to inputs.
column2:
An output parameter copies a value back into a caller variable. For example, one call can populate variables for both subtotal and tax.
Review source

column1: A stored procedure can both modify permanent data and return {{c1::result sets}} to its caller.
column2:
A SELECT inside the procedure can send rows to the client after the write. Those rows are not directly usable as a table source in another SELECT.
Review source

column1: To compute a shipping-cost value inside a SELECT list, choose a {{c1::scalar user-defined function}}.
column2:
The function returns one number for each evaluated set of inputs. That value fits in the SELECT list alongside the shipment's other fields.
Review source

column1: Return parameterized customer orders directly to a JOIN with a {{c1::table-valued function}}.
column2:
The function takes parameters and supplies rows for the join. A procedure can return rows to a caller but cannot be used directly in that position.
Review source

column1: When a parameterized table result needs only one SELECT query, prefer an {{c1::inline table-valued function}}.
column2:
An inline TVF defines its result with one SELECT. The optimizer can combine that logic with filters and joins in the calling query.
Review source

column1: When a table-valued function needs procedural steps to populate its declared result table, use a {{c1::multi-statement TVF}}.
column2:
A multi-statement TVF fills a local result table in several steps. Fabric SQL database supports this form, while Fabric Warehouse supports inline TVFs instead.
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column1: To record Salary changes automatically when UPDATE statements modify employee rows, use a {{c1::DML trigger}}.
column2:
Read old salaries from deleted and new salaries from inserted. UPDATE(Salary) alone tells you about the attempted write, not whether the values differ.
Review source

column1: For a simple allowed-value rule, prefer a {{c1::CHECK constraint}} over a trigger.
column2:
For example, a CHECK can reject a negative quantity without custom trigger code. Use a trigger only when an appropriate declarative rule cannot do the job.
Review source

column1: For explicitly called logic requiring TRY...CATCH and transaction control, choose a {{c1::stored procedure}}.
column2:
A procedure can catch errors and decide whether to commit or roll back. A T-SQL UDF cannot contain TRY...CATCH or take control of a transaction.
Review source

column1: On large inputs, a non-inlined scalar UDF in WHERE can add overhead from repeated {{c1::per-row invocations}}.
column2:
Separate calls can accumulate when a filter evaluates the function for many rows. Inlining or a set-based rewrite can help if the actual plan shows that cost.
Review source

column1: SQL Server 2019 and later can transform eligible T-SQL scalar function calls through {{c1::scalar UDF inlining}}.
column2:
Inlining lets the optimizer see the eligible function's logic instead of calling it separately. The database, function, and individual call must all qualify.
Review source

column1: A nonindexed view and the statement that uses it share {{c1::one execution plan}} when SQL Server compiles that statement.
column2:
The nonindexed view supplies query text, not an independently compiled or cached result. SQL Server can cache the plan for the statement that uses it.
Review source

column1: A UDF used in an indexed view expression must be {{c1::deterministic}}.
column2:
A deterministic function produces the same result for the same inputs and state. Indexed views also require schema binding and restrict data and external access.
Review source
